Jyoti waited until the evening, when her mother Kavitha had finished milking the buffaloes and sat on the charpai in the courtyard.

"Amma, I need to tell you something."

Kavitha looked up, already worried.

"I've been offered a place in the nursing course in Jaipur. I'm going to take it."

"Jaipur? And your marriage? Your father's plans?"

Jyoti took her mother's rough hand. "Amma, I know you want the best for me. You've worked in the fields every day so I could study. I'm grateful, more than I can say. But this is the path I've chosen. I'd like your blessing. And if it goes badly, I'll carry it. Not you."

Kavitha was quiet a long time. The buffalo shifted in its shed.

"You talk like your grandmother," she said at last. "She also never listened to anyone." But she was almost smiling.

For twenty years, I made every decision for Lokesh. Which school, which tuition, which friends were suitable. I thought that was my job.

When he told me last year that he wanted to leave engineering and train as a chef, I wanted to forbid it. I even rehearsed the speech.

But something stopped me. Maybe it was his face. He wasn't asking permission. He was telling me, gently, as one adult tells another.

So instead of the speech, I asked questions. Where will you train? How will you manage money? What will you do if it's hard? He had answers for most of them.

I told him I was worried. I told him I'd help if he asked. And then I let him go.

Last week he cooked for us, a full dinner, in his tiny rented kitchen. I watched him move around that stove like he belonged there. I was prouder than I've ever been.

— Nirmala

qa.q: What did Lokesh want to train as?
qa.a: A chef.

qa.q: How did Nirmala feel watching Lokesh cook last week?
qa.a: Nirmala felt prouder than ever, seeing him confident and at home in his own kitchen.

qa.q: What did Nirmala do instead of forbidding Lokesh's choice?
qa.a: Nirmala asked questions, shared the worry, offered help if asked, and let Lokesh make the decision.

qa.q: How might Lokesh have felt when Nirmala asked questions instead of giving a speech?
qa.a: He probably felt respected and relieved, treated as an adult.

grounding: Nirmala shifts from decision-maker to adviser for Lokesh, accepting he may err, and learns to be proud of his independence.

Family counsellor's note, final session

Rekha first came in March, distressed that her daughter Seema, twenty, had moved into a shared flat in Pune against her wishes. "She doesn't need me anymore," she said then.

Over the sessions, Rekha has worked on changing her role. She described three changes today. First, she now asks Seema, "Do you want my advice?" before giving it. Second, when Seema chose a college course Rekha disagreed with, Rekha said her piece once and then stopped. Third, when Seema's first month's budget went wrong, Rekha did not say "I told you so"; she only asked what Seema had learned.

Today Rekha said, "She calls me more now, not less. She asks what I think." She was smiling. "I think I'm actually proud of her for leaving."

I have closed our sessions.

— Anjali Kulkarni, counsellor

qa.q: Where did Seema move to?
qa.a: A shared flat in Pune.

qa.q: How does Rekha feel now compared with March?
qa.a: In March she felt distressed and unneeded; now she feels proud of Seema's independence and happier, smiling.

qa.q: Which of Rekha's changes helped most, and why?
qa.a: Asking before advising, saying her piece once, and not saying "I told you so" helped, because they let her become an adviser rather than a decision-maker.

qa.q: How has Seema responded to her mother's new role?
qa.a: Seema calls more, not less, and asks what Rekha thinks, showing the relationship of two adults is growing.

grounding: A counsellor's note shows Rekha shifting from decision-maker to adviser for her adult daughter, accepting mistakes, and becoming proud of her independence.

passage:
It was forty-four degrees in Jodhpur, the power had gone, and there was exactly one mango left in the fridge.

Ammi cut it in two. Samir looked at his half, then at Kashish's.

"Hers is bigger!"

"It is NOT!"

"It is! Look, the seed side is mine!"

Kashish held hers up. "Fine, you got the seed. But you got the later bedtime last week. And the new school bag."

"You got the window seat on the bus to Nani's!"

Ammi put the knife down. They weren't really arguing about mango. They'd been keeping score for weeks: bedtimes, bags, seats, who got the first roti.

She sat down between them. "Do you both think I love the other one more?"

Neither answered. But both of them stopped chewing.

qa.q: How hot was it in Jodhpur?
qa.a: Forty-four degrees.

qa.q: What are Samir and Kashish really worried about underneath the mango argument?
qa.a: Both feel anxious that they might matter less than the other, so they keep score of every share.

qa.q: What does Ammi do that gets to the real issue?
qa.a: She sits between them and asks if they think she loves the other more, naming the feeling under the fairness counting.

qa.q: How might Kashish feel when Ammi asks her question?
qa.a: She may feel caught and a little relieved, since the question touches what she really worries about.

grounding: On a hot day Samir and Kashish fight over mango halves, bedtimes and seats, keeping score because each needs to know they matter as much.

grounding: Jaya and Indu count phones, bedtimes and cake, demanding equality, because underneath each needs to know she matters as much.
